title: The Curse of Dimensionality
description: Explanation about why increasing the number of features can degrade performance and how to mitigate it.
content:
**The curse of dimensionality** refers to the phenomenon where some machine learning algorithms deteriorate in their performance as the number of features (i.e. dimensions) increases.

There are several key aspects of this phenomenon:
• Data sparsity
• Distance concentration
• Overfitting and the Hughes phenomenon

In high-dimensional spaces, data points become increasingly sparse. For instance, if you try to sample a space uniformly, the number of points required to maintain a given density grows exponentially with the number of dimensions. This sparsity makes it difficult to estimate reliable statistical properties of the data, since there isn't enough data to "fill" the space sufficiently.

Many algorithms rely on distance calculations (e.g., in K-Nearest Neighbors or clustering methods). However, as dimensions increase, the notion of distance loses its discriminatory power. Distances between points tend to converge, making it challenging to distinguish between close and far away points. This phenomenon not only increases computational costs but can also degrade performance, since the relative differences that help discriminate classes vanish.

When the number of features is high but the number of samples is limited, models can easily overfit by capturing noise rather than the underlying signal. This is sometimes related to the Hughes phenomenon, where adding more features initially can improve performance up to a point, after which performance degrades because the model begins to fit the noise.

To combat the curse of dimensionality, several strategies are commonly employed:
• Dimensionality reduction
• Feature selection
• Regularization
• Data preprocessing or normalization
